items.stem: Why should you define access patterns before designing a DynamoDB table?

options.text: Key and index design depend on how data is queried
options.rationale: Correct: DynamoDB is designed around access patterns; keys and indexes follow from them.

options.text: DynamoDB auto-creates joins from the schema
Access patterns set the billing currency
options.rationale: Access patterns are unrelated to billing currency.

options.text: Tables cannot be queried without a full scan
options.rationale: Well-designed keys and indexes allow efficient queries without scans.

items.explanation: Correct: DynamoDB is designed around access patterns; keys and indexes follow from them.

items.stem: A routine lookup of a customer's orders currently uses Scan and is slow and costly. What is the better approach?

options.text: Query a key or secondary index matching the access pattern
options.rationale: Correct: Query reads only matching items; Scan reads the whole table.
Scanning more often increases cost without fixing the pattern.

options.text: Add more attributes to each item
options.rationale: Item size does not turn a Scan into an efficient lookup.

options.text: Switch the table to a relational engine mid-request
options.rationale: You cannot swap engines per request; redesign the access pattern instead.

items.explanation: Correct: Query reads only matching items; Scan reads the whole table.

items.stem: Which TWO help mitigate a hot partition in DynamoDB? (Select TWO.)

options.rationale: Correct: a high-cardinality key spreads load across partitions.

options.text: Add a write-sharding suffix to the key
options.rationale: Correct: sharding distributes writes that would otherwise hit one partition.

options.text: Store all items under a single constant key
options.rationale: A constant key concentrates all load on one partition.
Removing indexes does not address key distribution.

items.explanation: Correct: a high-cardinality key and write-sharding both spread load and relieve hot partitions.
